facts.statehood_note: Ratified the U.S. Constitution; New Jersey was the third state to ratify it and the first to approve the Bill of Rights.

symbols.name: Blueberry (made official in 2004 after a campaign by fourth graders in Brick)

facts.name_origin: Named in 1664 after the Isle of Jersey in the English Channel; the Lenape name for the land is Scheyichbi.

government.chambers: New Jersey Senate (40 senators) and New Jersey General Assembly (80 members)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; after two terms in a row a governor must wait before running again), elected together with a lieutenant governor, an office added to the constitution by amendment.
government.courts: New Jersey Supreme Court (a chief justice and six associate justices).
government.constitution: Constitution of 1947, which strengthened the governor's office, streamlined the courts, ordered desegregation of schools and the National Guard years before the national civil rights movement, and guaranteed workers' right to organize. New Jersey's first constitution (1776) let property owners vote, including single women and free Black men, until an 1807 law limited voting to white men.
government.kid_line: "No person shall be denied the enjoyment of any civil or military right, nor be discriminated against in the exercise of any civil or military right, nor be segregated in the militia or in the public schools, because of religious principles, race, color, ancestry or national origin." (New Jersey Constitution, Article I, paragraph 5)

long_ago.about: Ancestors of the Lenape have lived in New Jersey for more than 10,000 years; about 8,000 Indigenous people lived here in the 1600s. They grew maize (corn), planting in March, and also hunted, fished, and gathered. Families belonged to clans traced through the mother, grouped under the Turtle, Turkey, and Wolf.
Lenape communities in the north spoke Munsee. Along the Hackensack River, a Dutch visitor in the 1630s saw 100 or more men stand in a long line and drive deer toward the river.
Lenape communities in the south spoke Unami. They gathered huge amounts of fish and shellfish from the bays and harvested clams all year round in southern New Jersey.

today.about: State-recognized tribe; New Jersey's Attorney General affirmed its state recognition in a 2018 settlement after the tribe went to court.
State-recognized tribe; New Jersey has recognized it since 1980, and the Attorney General reaffirmed this in 2019.
State-recognized tribe (recognized since 1980, reaffirmed in 2019); it lost its former home at the Rankokus Reservation (now Rancocas State Park) and continues its traditions and cultural teaching.

first_peoples.today_note: New Jersey recognizes three tribes (state recognition); none is federally recognized, and in 2011 a state letter wrongly said New Jersey had no recognized tribes, which the state corrected in 2018 and 2019. Under the 1758 Treaty of Easton and later pressure, most Lenape were pushed west into Pennsylvania, Ohio, and beyond; the federally recognized Lenape nations today are the Delaware Nation and the Delaware Tribe of Indians, both in Oklahoma, plus the Stockbridge-Munsee Community in Wisconsin.
sites: Indian Mills in Shamong Township (once called Brotherton), where the colony set up a 3,258-acre reservation in 1758 for the few Lenape families still in New Jersey; by about 1800 most families had left for New York or the West.

history.event: Indigenous people, including ancestors of the Lenape, are living on the land now called New Jersey.
About 8,000 Indigenous people live in New Jersey. A Dutch settler in 1628 records that the Lenape plant their main crop, maize, in March.

Henry Hudson charts the coast. The Dutch build New Netherland along the Hudson, Raritan, and Passaic rivers, and the Swedes settle along the Delaware River. Trade with the Lenape for furs begins, but war and new diseases harm Lenape communities.

Europeans bring enslaved and free Africans. English rules reward enslavers with 60 acres of land for each enslaved person brought in. By 1776, African Americans, mostly enslaved, are 12 percent of the colony's people.
England takes over the region, and it is named New Jersey after the Isle of Jersey. It is later split into East and West Jersey, then reunited as one royal colony in 1702.

In the Treaty of Easton, the Lenape are required to move west out of New Jersey and New York. The colony sets up the Brotherton reservation, 3,258 acres at Indian Mills, for the few Lenape families still in New Jersey.

Washington's army wins at Trenton, a turning point of the Revolution. More than 600 battles and skirmishes are fought in New Jersey, more than anywhere else. The first state constitution lets property owners vote, including single women and free Black men.
On December 18, New Jersey becomes the third state to ratify the U.S. Constitution. Its delegate William Paterson's 'New Jersey Plan' led to equal representation of every state in the U.S. Senate.

New Jersey passes a law to end slavery only gradually: it applies only to children born to enslaved people in 1804 or later, so many people stay enslaved. An 1807 law takes away the vote from women and Black men.

New Jersey is a passageway on the Underground Railroad and home to many free Black people. Levin and Sidney Still escape slavery in Maryland and settle in New Jersey; their son William Still helps hundreds of freedom seekers.
William Parker Foulke digs up Hadrosaurus foulkii in a Haddonfield marl pit, the first nearly complete dinosaur skeleton ever found.
New Jersey, the only Union state Lincoln lost twice, still records over 88,000 enlistments for the Union, including about 2,900 Black soldiers in the U.S. Colored Infantry.
After first refusing to ratify the Thirteenth Amendment, New Jersey becomes the last northern state to end slavery. In 1868 it even tries to take back its approval of the Fourteenth Amendment.
On March 31, Thomas Mundy Peterson of Perth Amboy becomes the first African American in the nation to vote under the new Fifteenth Amendment.

trailblazers.name: William Still
trailblazers.group: Black American man, Underground Railroad leader
trailblazers.text: Born free in Burlington County to parents who had escaped slavery, William Still directed the Vigilance Committee of Philadelphia, which helped fund Harriet Tubman's rescues, and built a network of safe houses from the South to Canada. He interviewed hundreds of freedom seekers, once discovering that one was his own long-lost brother, and published their stories in his book The Underground Railroad.

trailblazers.name: Dr. James Still
trailblazers.text: Another member of the Still family, Dr. James Still became a well-known herbalist in Medford, treating patients with medicines made from plants. By the time of his death he was the third largest landowner in Burlington County.

trailblazers.name: Thomas Mundy Peterson
trailblazers.text: On March 31, 1870, Thomas Mundy Peterson of Perth Amboy became the first African American in the nation to vote under the Fifteenth Amendment, a historic first step in a long struggle for equal voting rights.

trailblazers.name: Elizabeth Coleman White
trailblazers.text: Working on her family's cranberry farm at Whitesbog, Elizabeth White partnered with scientist Frederick Coville to grow wild blueberries as a crop. In 1916 they produced the first cultivated blueberry harvest, which is why the blueberry is New Jersey's state fruit.

trailblazers.name: Alice Paul
trailblazers.text: Alice Paul of Moorestown was a leader in the fight for the Nineteenth Amendment, which gave women the right to vote in 1920. Then she started a new campaign for a constitutional amendment guaranteeing equal rights regardless of sex.

trailblazers.name: Larry Doby
trailblazers.text: Larry Doby of Paterson became the second African American to play Major League Baseball, in 1947, helping to break the color barrier in the sport.

landforms: High Point (1,803 feet), the highest place, in Sussex County
Kittatinny Ridge, cut by the Delaware Water Gap
The Palisades, steep cliffs along the Hudson River
Pine Barrens, a huge pine-and-oak forest in the south
126 miles of Atlantic beaches from Sandy Hook to Cape May
waters: Delaware River (western border), the longest free-flowing river east of the Mississippi
Great Falls of the Passaic in Paterson
Over 400 public lakes, ponds, and reservoirs
geography.regions: Northwestern New Jersey (the Skylands) is wooded and mountainous, the Pine Barrens cover the southern interior, and the Jersey Shore lines the Atlantic coast.

ecosystems.name: Pine Barrens
ecosystems.about: Over a million acres of forests, farms, and wetlands in seven southern counties, mostly covered with pine and oak. In 1978 Congress made it the country's first National Reserve, and it is a U.S. Biosphere Reserve.

ecosystems.name: Coastal salt marshes and bays
ecosystems.about: Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge protects more than 48,000 acres of coast, 78 percent salt marsh, on the Atlantic Flyway, a major bird migration route. The knobbed whelk, the state shell, lives in New Jersey's bays.

ecosystems.name: Streams and freshwater swamps
ecosystems.about: The brook trout, the state fish, can only live in clean water, so finding one means the water is healthy. Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge, just 26 miles from Times Square, is a rest stop for migrating waterfowl.

science.weather: New Jersey has hot summers and cold winters, with 43 to 51 inches of rain and snow a year. Nor'easters can bring blizzards and flooding. Hurricanes and tropical storms are less common but serious: Sandy came ashore near Brigantine on October 29, 2012, as a post-tropical storm with sustained winds of about 80 mph (70 knots).
science.resources: Once known for farms (the 'Garden State'), ceramics in Trenton, and glass in South Jersey, New Jersey today leads in advanced manufacturing, telecommunications, biotechnology, and pharmaceuticals. The state microbe, found in New Jersey soil, was used at Rutgers to make the medicine streptomycin.
science.highlight: Dinosaurs and discoveries: Hadrosaurus foulkii, found in Haddonfield in 1858, was the first nearly complete dinosaur fossil. New Jersey scientists also won a Nobel Prize for finding the faint echo of the Big Bang.

g3_ss.plan: The Lenape of Scheyichbi: corn planting, clam gathering, Turtle, Turkey, and Wolf clans; Lenape nations in New Jersey today.

g3_ss.title: New Jersey Trailblazers

g45_ss.title: New Jersey's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Munsee and Unami Lenape homelands, seasonal life, and how the fur trade, disease, Brotherton, and the 1758 Treaty of Easton changed Lenape life.

g45_ss.title: Colony and Crossroads of the Revolution
g45_ss.plan: Dutch, Swedish, and English colonies; slavery and the 60-acre rule; Trenton and Morristown; the 1776 constitution that let some women and free Black men vote; the New Jersey Plan.

g45_ss.title: Freedom Slowly Won, 1804–1870
g45_ss.plan: Gradual abolition, the 1807 voting rollback, the Still family and the Underground Railroad, the Civil War, the 1866 end of slavery, and Thomas Mundy Peterson's vote.

g3_sci.title: Dinosaur in a Marl Pit
g3_sci.plan: Hadrosaurus and how fossils are found and rebuilt; make a fossil impression.

g3_sci.title: Blueberries and Bogs
g3_sci.plan: How blueberries and cranberries grow in wet, sandy Pine Barrens soil; the story of the first cultivated blueberries.

g3_sci.title: Clean Water Clues
g3_sci.plan: Brook trout and stream bugs as signs of healthy water; test local water and talk about pollution.

g45_sci.title: Coastal Storms and the Shore
g45_sci.plan: Nor'easters, hurricanes like Sandy, and how barrier beaches and salt marshes protect the coast.

g45_sci.title: Birds on the Atlantic Flyway
g45_sci.plan: Track migrating birds through Forsythe and Great Swamp refuges and map why wetlands matter.

g45_sci.title: Microbes and Medicine
g45_sci.plan: The state microbe and streptomycin: how scientists found a medicine in soil, and a safe classroom model of how microbes grow.
